After episode 1 “kernel implementation bugs are annoying” of the “The autumn of sound checkers” I present episode 2 “runtime bugs are annoying too”…

On the heel of con-leche follows con-ron, a line-by-line port of con-leche to Rust, including an equivalence proof peformed in Aeneas.

By running both con-leche and con-ron on your proofs the danger of possible bugs in the Lean runtime or compiler is greatly dimished.

Amazing! But something to emphasize is that having verified checkers is only good if they are used. Like if Palomar, say, doesn’t use these checkers then they aren’t doing much to verify the flood of oncoming AI Math.
Also verified byte code checker when? :smile: (I’m being serious.)
(1) How does con-ron verify bignum calculations? In con-leche they were hidden in the lean runtime. Does Aeneas similarly hide them or are they verified?

(2) How trustworthy is Aeneas? In particular, if you super optimized con-ron to not be a line-by-line port of con-leche but instead a heavily optimized Lean checker (borrowing ideas from Nanoda), would you trust the proof of functional equivalence to still hold in practice if Aeneas says it does formally?

Jason Rute schrieb:

(1) How does con-ron verify bignum calculations? In con-leche they were hidden in the lean runtime. Does Aeneas similarly hide them or are they verified?

Bignum isn't so hard if you don't need the last iota (heh) of performance, so it has its own (simple) verified bignum library.

Or, in Claude's words

ron::Nat was written from scratch on the 12th and proved on the 13th: 987 lines of Rust, 2 307 lines of Lean, no upstream source to cite, since it replaces the runtime's GMP rather than porting anything.

What it is: a bare little-endian vector of 64-bit limbs, normalised (last limb non-zero), with zero, one, conversion from and to a word, comparison, beq/ble/blt, add, sub, predecessor, multiplication by a word and by a number, power, division with remainder, gcd, the three bitwise operations, both shifts, and the hash the memo tables key on. The algorithms are deliberately the simplest that are correct: schoolbook multiplication as shift-and-add, and restoring long division one bit at a time. The file says why: Knuth's algorithm D would be faster and much harder to prove.

What "verified" means there: the abstraction is one recursive function, toNat l = x + 2⁶⁴ · toNat rest, and every operation has a homomorphism lemma against Lean's own Nat in the shape the rest of the tier uses, for example that a successful div_mod returns the pair abstracting to a / b and a % b, with normalisation preserved; the censuses on add_refines, div_refines, land_refines are pinned at the three standard axioms. The lemmas are partial in the usual way: if an operation fails in the model, which only an arithmetic overflow of an index could cause, the checker declines and nothing is claimed.

Two consequences worth knowing. The representation was chosen for the proof, not for speed: the design note records that a small/big enum would have quartered nothing and quadrupled the lemma count, and that a small-value fast path can be added later as a provably equal special case if profiling ever asks. It has not asked: kernel literals are small in practice, and the Mathlib instruction count sits below con-leche's. And the trusted base is exactly what the README says: the checker carries its own bignum, so a GMP bug is out of the picture on the Rust side.
(2): i don't know. But if I'd super optimize this, I'd do it on the Lean model first, and leave only the mechanical correspondence proof to Aeneas.

To expand on this:

My gut feeling is that it's preferable if the proof that relates Aeneas outputted lean to the spec lean function is as mechanical as possible, as that is large by volume. Having that proof do more than just validation the translation likely increases proof burden a lot. So i'd separate optimizations (I.e. genuinely different code paths) into a separate refinement and proof. And that's likely easier on the hand-written-lean-side than the rust side (my hypothesis, but without evidence).

Of course if there are optimizations that can only be done on the rust side things change.

And I don't have much experience with Aeneas yet, so maybe I'm overly cautious here.
I think overly cautious is good here.
2 messages were moved from this topic to #AI authored projects > comparator in the TCB by Joachim Breitner.

Joachim Breitner said:

By running both con-leche and con-ron on your proofs the danger of possible bugs in the Lean runtime or compiler is greatly dimished.

Can you clarify this? Does running both con-leche and con-ron add any more confidence than only running con-ron? Assuming that the Aeneas proof is correct, con-ron refines con-leche, so a proof passing con-ron will always pass con-leche (although the converse does not necessarily hold).

Unless I'm misunderstanding something, isn't running con-leche just a waste of CPU cycles if you've already checked with con-ron?
Well, you say it - assuming Aeneas proof translation is correct.
Plus there is always the unverified IO edge - reading files, printing results etc.
And then there is the remaining risk of compiler bugs, runtime bugs

This verified bignum library should be faster than bignum itself.
https://github.com/spitters/nanoda-verified-bignum

I was unhappy with con-ron: Verified code shouldn't be slower than unverified code, and I disliked that I had to use Rust’s unsafe to implement some pointer tagging to make perf reasonable.

So the term representation is now completely rewritten. It follows nanoda’s lead and cons-hashes expressions and put them into one big data structure (the DAG), with two tiers (a persistent one and a scratch tier for the per-declaration intermediates) and an EIdx (a u32) pointing into that data structure, with one bit indicating which tier to use.

To further refine this approach, our DAG does not store an enum ExprView. Rust sizes enums by the largest member, which is wasteful when most nodes are Expr.app. Instead, we have one array per constructor, with just the fields stored there, and the EIdx reserves four bits to indicate which constructor this is. This leads to very compact, uniform arrays and some operations (e.g. is_app) can be resolved without dereferencing. Names, levels, level lists and binder data are also hash-consed.

(There were other, less notable, performance tweaks of course).

This gave a 2× speedup (as measured by the arena), and it is catching up with nanoclo.

It also demonstrates that the combination of Rust, Aeneas and Lean can lead to pretty good results.

BTW, in particular interesting for @Sebastian Graf , this is relying on mvcgen to automate some of the proofs. In Claude’s own words:

Where and how. mvcgen (from Std.Do) is the workhorse of Theorem 1 and almost nowhere else. About 560 calls sit in some 56 files under Bridge/**, mostly the Core tier's walks and arms and the ExprOps specs, plus two in Arena/. The twin is written in a StateT-over-Except monad (AM). Each twin function gets a Hoare-triple spec registered with @[spec], stating what it does to the store and what the result denotes. A walk's refinement proof is then typically mvcgen [<the walk>] followed by one closer, usually grind, over the pure verification conditions that are left. The early spike (task #97s) settled this route. A ten-constructor walk with a memo, a cutoff and fuel was 13 lines of proof over 61 generated verification conditions, and one grind closed 60 of them. The same kind of theorem by hand would have been an estimated 200–350 lines, and finding the right simp only set for the monad took nine attempts. Theorem 2 deliberately does not use it. It has only 2 mentions in Refine2, because the lockstep design uses Aeneas-style progress stepping through our own lockstep tactic. There, the Rust's next call selects the lemma, so a divergence between Rust and twin shows up as a goal stuck at the exact bind where the programs part. A verification-condition generator would instead leave an unprovable condition far from its cause.

Experience. Good overall: once a function had its spec, a walk's proof was usually just "mvcgen plus closer". The cost is grind, not mvcgen: with every condition left as sorry, generating them was 2–6 % of elaboration time. The lessons, recorded in DESIGN.md as rules:

  • A registered @[spec] is a commitment. [spec] can't be erased, and passing a better lemma in mvcgen's own list doesn't override a registered one. So a spec that is too weak, for example one missing a frame conjunct, can't be worked around from the caller. We paid for that once with copies of function bodies, and fixed it by adding the frame conjunct to the spec. The rule since: state the frame the first time.
  • Specs have to be in the shape mvcgen produces. That includes the orientation of the postcondition's equations.
  • Existential witnesses need care. mvcgen must guess witnesses such as a denotation. When a spec names one as a parameter, it guesses wrong: in one case it picked the comparand instead of the term just interned.
  • Big walks need staging. They produce conditions with 40–60 inaccessible hypotheses, so we name and stage the facts before mvcgen instead of calling it once on the whole body.
  • Its cost grows with the number of arms in a dispatcher, about 1 s per arm.
  • There's a universe-metavariable trap with Spec.throw on Except.

None of these blocked us, but each cost a round before it became a rule.
